case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 23.12.2014 passed by the International Crimes Tribunal No.2, Dhaka in ICT-BD (ICT-2) Case No.04 of 2013)
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain CJ. This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 16.09.2015 passed by High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2622 of 2010 making the Rule absolute.

2. The facts, leading to the filing of this civil appeal, in a nutshell, are:

3. Respondent No. 1 herein, predecessor of respondent Nos.2 to 7 and respondent Nos.8 to 12 as the plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.27 of 1986 before the then Court of Upazila Munsif, Begumgonj on 03.02.1986 impleading the appellant Government of Bangladesh, respondent Nos.13 to 18 and Jalal Uddin, father of present respondent No.19 as defendants for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession.

<u>4. The plaintiffs' case, in short, is that their grandfather Moulvi Serajul Hoq Khan was the owner of the suit land. The then Government acquired more than 600 acres of land at Begumgonj, including 13 acres of land of Serajul Hoq Khan in L.A. Case No.6 of 1941-42. Serajul Hoq Khan took part of the compensation money on 15.2.1943 under protest and did not take the balance money which remained as revenue deposit. The Government did not evict the owners from the acquired land and said Serajul Hoq Khan remained in possession of his 13 acres of land, including dwelling house, garden, tanks etc. The Government ultimately did not use the land for the purpose of which it was acquired and by order dated 10.06.1955 ordered that the acquired lands including 'Ka' schedule land be given by way of lease to the former owners or their heirs on year to year basis upon executing an agreement for the same. Accordingly, all the ex-owners and their heirs including Makbul Hoq Khan, the father of the plaintiffs took year to year lease upon executing an agreement for 'Ka' schedule land. In 1975 the Government decided to return the acquired lands on condition that the former owners or their heirs would refund the compensation money which they took from the Government. This decision was communicated by the Land Ministry to defendant No.3-Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) in Memo No.6-38/75 dated 31.01.1975. Accordingly, Mukbul Hoq Khan, father of the plaintiffs filed a petition dated 05.04.1975 addressed to defendant No. 2-Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali for return of the 'Ka' schedule land to him. Defendant No. 3 by Memo No. 2749 SA dated 23.09.1975 reported to the Ministry of Land that 'Ka' schedule land might be returned to Mukbul Hoq Khan upon refund of the compensation money taken by Serajul Hoq Khan. Ultimately, the land having not been returned to the plaintiffs, they were compelled to file the suit.</u>

5. Defendant Nos. 1 to 4 and 5 to 8 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement contending, inter alia, that after completion of the process of acquisition the suit land vested in the Government and the plaintiffs as year to year lessees have been in possession of the suit land, but the lease has not been renewed for many years. It was further contended that the 'Kha' schedule land was leased out on the application of defendant No. 5 for establishing Jalal Uddin Mohila College.

6. The trial Court upon consideration of the evidence and materials on record by the judgment and decree dated 23.07.2005 dismissed the suit. Against the said judgment and decree, the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No. 156 of 2005 before the learned Joint District Judge, Third Court, Noakhali, who by his judgment and order dated 06.05.2010 dismissed the appeal.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order of the appellate Court, the plaintiffs then preferred a revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No.2622 of 2010. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division by the judgment and order dated 16.09.2015 made the Rule absolute.

8. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the defendants as the leave-petitioners filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.3202 of 2015 before this Division and obtained leave on 21.01.2016 resulting in Civil Appeal No.187 of 2016.

9. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Attorney General, appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that admittedly, the suit land was acquired in L.A. Case No. 06 of 1941-42 by the Government and the plaintiffs failed to prove that their grandfather, Serajul Hoq Khan, was owner of the suit land or the suit land was acquired from his possession. He further submits that the plaintiffs claim that their grandfather “উক্ত ভূমি অর্জন করিয়া” constructed homestead but no piece of paper in support of it could be produced by the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs' grandfather could not prove title to and possession in the acquired suit land and their grandfather could not withdraw the entire assessed compensation money. He continues to submit that there were as many as five prayers in the plaint without any prayer for declaration of title and that the suit land as shown in 'Gaf schedule for recovery of khas possession was vague and unspecified. He then submits that the definite case of the defendants is that the suit was not maintainable as it is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the High Court Division fell into error as it failed to consider the aforesaid legal and factual aspects of the case. Therefore, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. He then submits that the High Court Division misread and misinterpreted the evidence and materials on record and erred in reversing concurrent decisions of the Courts below without adverting to the findings of the Courts below. With reference to the letter dated 09.02.1987 (exhibit-15), he submits that High Court Division misread and misinterpreted the aforesaid letter of the Ministry of Land which is a interministerial correspondence and decision for de-requisition of acquired land can be taken only in cabinet meeting. He then submits that admittedly the suit land was acquired and it completely vested in the Government free from all encumbrances.

10. In respect of the college, the learned Attorney General, submits that it was established on 'Kha' schedule land and defendant No.5 paid Tk. 4,01,497/-as lease money and possession was delivered by the Government to the college and lease deed could not be registered as the suit is pending and the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Cumilla, on being satisfied that the college fulfilled the required criteria gave affiliation to the college and the National University also gave recognition to the college.

11. Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent Nos.1-12 of Civil Appeal No.187 of 2016 and the respondents of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.3203 of 2015, on the other hand, submits that admittedly, the suit land belonged to the plaintiffs' grandfather, Serajul Hoq Khan and that as the property was not used for the purpose for which it was acquired the Ministry of Land by exhibit-15 directed to release the suit land from acquisition and to handover possession thereof to the plaintiffs and as such, no interference is called for. He further submits that the acquisition was made by the then Government under the Land Acquisition Act No. 1 of 1894 and as such, the trial Court and the appellate Court fell in error as both the Courts below considered the case with reference to (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act,1948 and as such, no interference is called for.

12. Mr. Abul Kalam Chowdhury, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent No.13 of the Civil Appeal No.187 of 2016 and leave-petitioner of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.3203 of 2015, supports the arguments advanced by Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud, learned Senior Advocate.

13. Before addressing the conflicting contentions of the learned Attorney General for the appellants and the learned Senior Advocate for respondent Nos.1-12, it would be pertinent to quote the following grounds, on which, leave was granted:

"Admittedly the-suit land was acquired in L.A. Case No. 06 of 1941-42 by the Government. The plaintiffs failed to prove that their grandfather Serajul Hoq Khan was owner of the suit land or the suit land was acquired from his possession. And in the plaint it was claimed that their grandfather “উক্ত ভূমি অর্জন করিয়া” but no piece of paper in support of it could be produced by the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs' grandfather could not prove title and possession in the acquired suit land and their grandfather could not draw the entire assessed compensation money as he had no title in the suit land. And there are five prayers in the plaint without any prayer for declaration of title. And the suit land as shown in 'Ga' schedule for recovery of khas possession was vague and unspecified and in this connection defendant-opposite party referred Order VII Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and decision in the case of Nazrul Islam Babul and others Vs. Shanti Rani Dhupi and others reported in 12 MLR (AD) page 105, and the definite case of the defendant that the suit was not maintainable as it is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the High Court Division fell into error as it failed to consider aforesaid legal and factual aspects of the suit and as such the impugned judgment and order is not legally tenable.

The High Court Division misread and misinterpreted the evidence and materials on record and erred in reversing concurrent decisions of the Courts below without controverting the findings of the Courts below. The High Court Division misread and misinterpreted the letter of the Ministry of Land dated 09.02.1987,- i.e. exhibit-15 which is interministerial correspondence and decision for derequisition of acquired land can be taken only in cabinet meeting and not by any person and in this connection decision in the case of Haji Aftab Uddin and others Vs Bangladesh and others reported in 17 BLD(AD) page 1 was cited, but the High .Court Division overlooked the same and thus committed error of law resulting miscarriage of justice. Admittedly the suit land was acquired land and it completely vested to the Government free from all encumbrances and the plaintiffs had no legal right to claim release of the properties unless the right is conferred on them by any statutory provision and the plaintiffs were not in possession of the suit land when it was leased out and possession was delivered to the college, and the defendants including the Deputy Commissioner rightly and legally passed the orders and findings of the High Court Division to the contrary are against materials on record and erroneous.

Admittedly the college was established on 'Khaf schedule land and defendant No. 5 paid salami money amounting to Tk. 4,01,497/-as lease money and possession was delivered by the Government to the college and lease deed could not be registered as the suit is pending and the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Cumilla, on being satisfied that the college fulfilled the required criteria gave affiliation to the college; National University also gave recognition to the college. The Government legally and rightly enlisted the college for Monthly Payment Order (MPO). The Government constructed multi-storied building of the college and thousands of students have been studying there but findings of the High Court Division to the contrary ignoring the counter affidavit filed by opposite party No. 7 are unwarranted and legally erroneous."

14. Admittedly, for establishment of District Headquarters of Noakhali District, the suit land and other lands were acquired by the Government but the Government shifted the establishment of

District Headquarters of Noakhali from the suit land and other acquired lands to Maijdee. The acquired suit land was stated to have been in possession of the plain-tiffs. Normally the Government took possession of acquired land but in the instant case, possession has not been taken over and compensation money has not been fully paid. The Government claimed that after acquisition the suit land vested in the Government free from all encumbrances and the title, if any, of private individuals of acquired land extinguished.

15. In the plaint, the plaintiffs admitted that the suit property was acquired in L.A. Case No.06 of 1941-1942 as shown in schedule-Ka to the plaint for establishment of District Headquarters of Noakhali. The plaintiffs also claimed that their grandfather Moulavi Serajul Hoq Khan was the owner of the 'Ka' schedule land.

16. The trial Court came to a finding that defendant No.4, Upazila Revenue Officer submitted a report to defendant No.3, Additional Deputy Commissioner, stating that the 'Ka' schedule land measuring 8.10 acres of which 4.75 acres of land were used by the plaintiffs for their dwelling houses, garden, tanks etc. and that the remaining land was nal land and that the plaintiffs' predecessor-in-interest was the owner of that land and that the said report (exhibit-16) was filed by the plaintiffs before the Court. The trial Court also found that the written statement of defendant Nos.1-4 and exhibit-16, reveal that the suit land belonged to the plaintiffs' predecessor-in-interest. The trial Court also found that the plaintiffs obtained lease of the suit land from the Government on year to year.

17. After acquisition, the ownership of the suit land devolved upon the Government and the Government would decide whether they would lease out the suit land to anybody or not. The trial Court noted that if the Government decides to settle the suit land, then settlement should be given to previous owner of the suit land. But the plaintiffs could not claim that the Government was bound to settle the suit land to the plaintiffs.

18. The appellate Court concurred with the findings and decision arrived at by the trial Court. The appellate Court came to the finding that the decisions taken pursuant to exhibits-12 and 15 are Administrative decisions and if anybody neglected in implementing those decision then the plaintiffs could seek redress to the higher authority but unless higher authority took any action the civil Court did not have the jurisdiction to give any relief to the plaintiffs.

19. The High Court Division came to a finding that the specific prayer of the plaintiffs is for declaration that the order dated 26.01.1986 passed by the Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali, was illegal, arbitrary and without jurisdiction and also for implementation of the decision of the Ministry of Land dated 09.02.1987 (exhibit-15). The High Court Division further came to a finding that it was an admitted position that the plaintiffs were in possession from before acquisition of the suit land which was acquired in L.A. Case No.06 of 1941-1942. The High Court Division held that apart from the so-called lease of 1959, there was no paper to show that the plaintiffs were lessees of the Government and rather the plaintiffs were in continuous and uninterrupted possession for more than 60 years and the Government did not take any step to evict the plaintiffs and as such on this score also the plaintiffs acquired title to the suit land. The High Court Division also came to the finding that from the records, it appeared that till date admittedly no lease deed had been executed and registered by the concerned authority in favour of the college and as such, recognition of the college by the Education Board and inclusion of the college in the MPO and construction of the building under development project of the Government were illegal and collusive.

20. Admittedly, the plaintiffs in clear terms stated that the suit land along with other land was acquired for development of District Headquarters of Noakhali in L.A. Case No.06 of 1941-1942. The plaintiffs also admitted in the plaint that as per decision of the Government, the then Collector, Mr. Pana Ullah Ahmed on 10.05.1955 passed an order that the property acquired for establishment of District Headquarters of Noakhali be given lease to the original owners or their legal representatives on year to year basis. The plaintiffs also admitted that from 1956 the plaintiffs' father stated obtaining lease of the 'Ka' schedule land from the Government and that they have been in possession thereof on payment of lease money and also by executing agreement.

21. It is contended that the order dated 26.01.1986 (exhibit-12) passed by the Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali, proposing lease in favour of the college was illegal, arbitrary and without jurisdiction and that the decision of the Ministry of Land dated 09.02.1987 for releasing the suit land form acquisition be implemented. Admittedly, the suit land was validly acquired in L.A. Case No.06 of 1941-1942. Unless the suit land is released from acquisition no right, title and interest of the plaintiffs accrued in that land and as such, the plaintiffs are not entitled to obtain a decree declaring the order dated 26.01.1986 (exhibit-12) issued by the Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali, proposing lease in favour of the college to be illegal and without jurisdiction.

22. Since the property was validly acquired and vested in the Government free from all encumbrances the plaintiffs do not have any right to pray for implementation of the decision of the Ministry of Land dated 09.02.1987. The High Court Division came to a finding that the plain-tiffs have been in possession of the suit land from before acquisition and that they continued to possess thereof and that the plaintiffs pursuant to their uninterrupted possession of the suit land for more than 60 years acquired title to the suit land. The High Court Division, however, did not mention that the plaintiffs acquired title to the suit land by adverse possession. But the above finding implies that the High Court Division tried to mean that the plaintiffs acquired title by adverse possession. Admittedly, the suit land was validly acquired by the Government in L.A. Case No.06 of 1941- 1942 and the suit was filed in 1986. Therefore, it appears that the plaintiffs could not prove their possession in the suit land from the date of acquisition for a continuous period of 60 years. Therefore, the above finding is erroneous and patently based on wrong calculation.

23. The trial Court and the appellate Court decided the case based upon the (Emergency) Requisition of the Property Act, 1948 but the acquisition in the disputed case property was made under Land Acquisition Act No.1 of 1894. In this connection, it is pertinent to quote section 12 of the Act of 1894 as under:

"12.-(1) Such award shall be filed in the Collector's office and shall, except as hereinafter provided, be final and conclusive evidence, as between the Collector and the persons interested, whether they have respectively appeared before the Collector or not, of the true area and value of the land, and the apportionment of the compensation among the persons interested.

(2) The Collector shall give immediate notice of his award to such of the persons interested as are not present personally or by their representatives when the award is made.

24. From the above section, it appears that the award filed in the Collector's office shall be final and conclusive evidence as between the Collector and the persons interested. It is immaterial whether the persons interested appeared before the Collector or not and the apportionment of the compensation among the persons interested. Section 16 of the Act of 1894 states that when the Collector has made an award under section 11, he may take possession of the land, which shall thereupon absolutely vest in the Government, free from all encumbrances. In the case in hand, the plaintiffs stated that the Collector assessed the compensation of the acquired land at Tk.11,592/- and that the plaintiffs' grandfather took Tk.5001/- on 15.02.1943 with objection and that the remaining amount was kept in the revenue department which plaintiffs did not withdraw.

25. The Act of 1894 in part-III provides for "Reference to Court and Procedure Thereon". Section 18(1) occurring in part-III provides that any person interested who has not accepted the award may, by written application to the Collector, require that the matter be referred by the Collector for the determination of the Court, whether his objection be to the measurement of the land, the amount of the compensation, the persons to whom it is payable, or the apportionment of the compensation among the persons interested. Part-III of the Act contains sections 18 to 28 which provide for addressing the grievances of the persons whose properties have been acquired by the Government. The plaintiffs could not produce any paper showing that their predecessor-in-interest had made attempt for a reference to the Court for the reliefs contained in sections 18 to 28 of the Act of 1894. Therefore, it appears that the plaintiffs' grandfather received Tk.5001/- with objection was not proved and nothing was produced by them showing that their grandfather made any attempt to vindicate his grievances before the Court as provided by Part-III of the Act of 1894.

26. In the light of the findings, we are of the view that the Government validly acquired the suit land along with other land for establishment of District Headquarters of Noakhali and that the acquired properties vested in the Government free from all encumbrances as provided under section 16 of the Act of 1894.

27. Once the property is validly acquired there is no scope for releasing the same. But as owner of the acquired property, the Government is at liberty to lease out the suit land to anybody. In the case in hand, the trial Court, the appellate Court and the High Court Division found that the plaintiffs had been in possession of a portion of the suit land and that their dwelling houses, garden, and tank are on the said land.

<u>28. Admittedly, the Government took decision to lease out 3.06 acres of land to the Jalal Uddin Mohila College, Begumgonj, Noakhali. The college was given recognition by the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education; Cumilla and also by the National University. The college has also been included in the Monthly Payment Order (MPO) of the Government and as part of its development scheme Government constructed a building of the college. The Government has decided to lease out 'Kha' schedule land measuring 3.06 acres of land out of the suit land to the said college for imparting education to thousands of students of that area. The plaintiffs do not have any right to challenge the decision of the Government to lease out the 'Kha' schedule land to the college. Moreover, they have not acquired any right in the suit land till date. If 3.06 acres of land shown in schedule 'Kha' are deducted from 'Ka' schedule land measuring 8.10 acres then 5.04 acres of land remain in possession of the plaintiffs.</u>

<u>29. Having gone through the records and the judgments of all the Courts, we find that the remaining 5.04 acres of land belonging to the grandfather of the plain-tiffs before acquisition may be leased out to them as their grandfather was stated to have withdrawn 50% of the lease money.</u>

<u>30. In the light of the findings made before, we are inclined to set aside the impugned judgment delivered by the High Court Division and allow the appeal with the direction that 5.04 acres of land may be leased out to the plaintiffs considering their prolong possession thereof.</u>

<u>31. Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.3203 of 2015 is disposed of in the light of the findings and decision made in the body of the judgment of this appeal.</u>

32. There is no order as to costs.

End.
